title: Interviews and Job Search Strategy
summary: Prepare STAR stories and technical answers, track applications, handle offers and set a 12-month career plan.
objectives: Build three STAR stories from your own experience.
Prepare for technical interviews with a repeatable method.
Track applications, evaluate offers and draft a 12-month plan.

explanation.heading: Interviews test evidence and thinking
explanation.body:
An interview is a structured conversation where the employer decides whether you can do the work and be taught. Earlier lessons covered your self-map, resume and online presence. The interview is where you prove them out loud. Interviewers use two kinds of questions: **behavioural** (tell me about a time you faced a deadline) and **technical** (explain a join, debug this code). Both reward clear thinking and honest answers more than memorised speeches.

Preparation should feel like building a small library you can draw from: a handful of stories, a set of core concepts you can explain, and a few questions for the interviewer.

explanation.heading: STAR stories
explanation.body:
**STAR** stands for Situation, Task, Action, Result. It keeps answers short and evidence-based. Situation: one sentence of context. Task: what you were responsible for. Action: what *you* did, step by step. Result: the outcome, with a number if possible, and what you learned.

**Worked example.** Question: "Tell me about a time you handled a problem in a team." Answer: "In our final-year project, our data kept duplicating (Situation). I owned the database layer (Task). I compared the insert logic, found a missing unique constraint, added it and wrote tests for three edge cases (Action). Duplicates dropped to zero and we presented without errors; I now check constraints early (Result)." Prepare three stories covering teamwork, a failure or mistake, and a challenge you overcame, then adapt them to different questions. Use "I" for your actions, and keep each to about ninety seconds.

explanation.heading: Technical interview preparation
explanation.body:
For a fresher aiming at ABAP, interviewers expect strong fundamentals: SQL joins and keys, programming logic, data types, loops and conditions, basic database design, and a first understanding of SAP: what it is, what ABAP does, and common objects such as reports, tables and enhancements. Build a list of 30 core questions and answer each aloud in about a minute.

Use a repeatable method: **define, example, trade-off**. Define the concept in a sentence, give a small example, mention when you would use it or where it fails. When you do not know, say so, then reason aloud: "I have not used that, but I think it works like..." Honest reasoning scores better than bluffing. Practise with a friend, or record yourself. Finally, prepare two thoughtful questions for them, such as what a fresher learns in the first three months.

explanation.heading: Tracking, offers and a 12-month plan
explanation.body:
Treat the job search like a small project. Keep a **tracker** with columns: company, role, date applied, source, contact, stage, next action and date, and result. Review it twice a week. Aim for steady effort, for example five tailored applications and two outreach messages weekly, and note what you learn from every rejection.

When an offer arrives, read the letter fully: role, location, pay structure, notice or service agreement terms, and joining date. Ask for clarity politely, then decide against your priorities. Finally, write a **12-month plan** with a quarterly goal each: for example, Q1 finish ABAP fundamentals and two projects, Q2 apply widely and practise interviews, Q3 join and learn the project, Q4 earn a first certification or take on a bigger task. Review it monthly and adjust.

examples.title: A STAR answer in ninety seconds
examples.body: Situation: Our group project had three people and one deadline. Task: I was in charge of testing. Action: I wrote a checklist of 20 test cases, ran them each evening and logged defects for the team. Result: We found 8 bugs before submission and scored full marks for functionality; I now start testing early.
examples.takeaway: The answer is short, uses "I", and ends with a result and a lesson.

examples.title: A simple tracker row
examples.body: Company: Alpha Tech. Role: ABAP trainee. Applied: 3 Oct. Source: referral. Stage: technical round done. Next action: send thank-you note and revise joins by 10 Oct. Result: pending.
examples.takeaway: A next action with a date keeps momentum and prevents dropped follow-ups.

exercises.prompt: What does the R in STAR stand for?
exercises.why: Result is the outcome and the lesson. Responsibility belongs to the Task step.

exercises.prompt: A repeatable method for explaining concepts is define, example and ____. (one word)
exercises.why: Mentioning the trade-off shows judgement, not only memory.

exercises.prompt: An interviewer asks about a concept you have never used. What is the best reply?

options.text: Pretend you know it and give a confident guess.
options.feedback: Bluffing is usually exposed by one follow-up question.

options.text: Say you have not used it, then reason from what you know about similar ideas.
options.feedback: Honesty plus visible reasoning shows trainability.

options.text: Stay silent until they move on.
options.feedback: Silence gives no evidence of thinking.

options.text: Change the topic to your project.
options.feedback: Redirecting may seem evasive without acknowledging the question.

exercises.why: Interviewers for freshers mainly test learning ability, so honest reasoning beats bluffing.

exercises.prompt: Write one STAR story, about 90 seconds spoken, from a team project, college event or past job. Label S, T, A and R and include a measurable or observable result and one lesson.

descriptors.1: STAR structure is vague or generic.
descriptors.2: STAR structure is clear but could be more specific.
descriptors.3: STAR structure is specific, concrete and well reasoned.

rubric.label: Your own actions in specific steps

descriptors.1: Your actions is vague or generic.
descriptors.2: Your actions is clear but could be more specific.
descriptors.3: Your actions is specific, concrete and well reasoned.

descriptors.1: Result and lesson is vague or generic.
descriptors.2: Result and lesson is clear but could be more specific.
descriptors.3: Result and lesson is specific, concrete and well reasoned.

exercises.modelAnswer: S: Our final-year project had duplicate student records. T: I owned the database layer. A: I compared insert logic, found no unique constraint, added one and wrote tests for three edge cases. R: Duplicates fell to zero and the demo ran cleanly; I now check constraints at design time.
exercises.guidance: Strong answers use "I", describe two or three concrete steps and end with a result and lesson. Common mistakes are long context, saying "we" throughout and omitting the result. Time yourself: more than two minutes is too long.

task.title: Launch your tracker and STAR library
task.brief: Set up a job-search tracker and write three STAR stories.
steps: Create a tracker with company, role, date, source, stage, next action and result.
Add at least five roles you plan to apply for.
Write three STAR stories: teamwork, mistake, challenge.
Practise one story aloud and time it.
checklist: Tracker has a next action for each row
One story timed under two minutes
I drafted a 12-month plan with quarterly goals
task.evidencePrompt: Paste your quarterly goals for the next 12 months.

quiz.prompt: Which part of STAR should hold the most detail?
quiz.why: Your actions are the evidence; context should be brief.

quiz.prompt: When you do not know an answer, the best move is to say so and then ____ aloud. (one word)
quiz.why: Reasoning aloud shows how you approach unknown problems.
A dated next action prevents follow-ups from being forgotten.
Quarterly goals are specific enough to act on, and monthly review lets you adapt.

bank.prompt: You are asked about a failure. Which approach is best?
options: Describe a real mistake, what you did to fix it and what you changed afterwards
bank.why: Owning a mistake and showing learning builds credibility.

bank.prompt: Which prep habit best improves technical answers?
options: Answering core questions aloud in about a minute each
bank.why: Speaking aloud tests whether you truly understand and builds fluency.

bank.prompt: After a rejection, what is most useful?
options: Note what you learned and update your preparation
bank.why: Capturing lessons turns rejections into improvement.

cards.back: Situation, Task, Action, Result: a short structure for stories. Spend most time on your own actions and end with a result and lesson.
Define, give a small example, then mention a trade-off or limit. If unsure, say so and reason aloud.

cards.front: What goes in a job-search tracker?
cards.back: Company, role, date, source, contact, stage, next action with date and result. Review it twice a week.

cards.front: How to build a 12-month career plan?
cards.back: One goal per quarter, such as learn, apply, join, deepen. Review monthly and adjust.

reflection: Which of your experiences would make the strongest STAR story, and what result can you point to?

keyPoints: STAR keeps answers short and evidence-based.
Define, example, trade-off; reason aloud when unsure.
A tracker with dated next actions keeps the search moving.
revision.redo: Say one STAR story aloud in under two minutes.
